title: Appendix A — Serialization and Compression Technical Details: Quality Question Bank

questions.question: Why does the book advise against using CSV in data pipelines despite its ubiquity?
options: CSV is highly error-prone (inconsistent delimiter/quote/escape conventions) and delivers poor performance — switching from CSV to Parquet has improved job performance by up to 100x
CSV files cannot be opened by any modern software tools
CSV is illegal to use for cross-organization data exchange under GDPR
CSV always requires a paid commercial license to use in production
questions.explanation: The book states: "Data engineers should avoid using CSV files in pipelines because they are highly error-prone and deliver poor performance," citing 100x speedups from switching to Parquet.

questions.question: What's the key structural difference between row-based and columnar serialization?
options: Row-based formats store each record/object as a complete unit written sequentially; columnar formats pivot storage so each column's values are grouped together in their own files
Row-based formats can only store numeric data, while columnar formats can only store text
There is no real structural difference — only a naming convention difference
Columnar formats store each record sequentially, while row-based formats group values by field
questions.explanation: The book explains row-oriented formats write "complete relations... sequentially," while "with columnar serialization, data organization is essentially pivoted by storing each column into its own set of files."

questions.question: Why does columnar storage typically pair so well with compression?
options: Storing similar values next to each other (all of one column's values together) creates high redundancy, which compression algorithms can exploit for strong ratios — e.g. tokenizing frequently repeated values
Columnar storage is required by law to use compression in most databases
Compression only works on row-based formats, never on columnar ones
Columnar storage makes compression entirely unnecessary, so it's rarely used
questions.explanation: The book explains: "Storing data as columns also puts similar values next to each other, allowing us to encode columnar data efficiently... columnar storage is usually combined with compression."

questions.question: Why are single-row updates especially expensive in a columnar storage system?
options: Changing one field means decompressing the relevant column file(s), modifying them, recompressing, and rewriting to storage — expensive compared to a row-oriented system's in-place update
Columnar systems are physically incapable of performing any updates whatsoever
Updates are actually cheaper in columnar systems than in row-oriented ones
Row-oriented systems have an identical update cost to columnar systems
questions.explanation: The book states: "To change one field in one record, we must decompress the column file, modify it, recompress it, and write it back to storage... the overhead for updating a single row is horrendous."

questions.question: What key advantage does Parquet offer over a database's proprietary internal columnar format (e.g. BigQuery's or Snowflake's own storage)?
options: Portability/interoperability — Parquet files can be read directly by many tools (Spark, Presto, etc.) without the performance hit of reserializing proprietary formats for external use
Parquet is always faster for internal queries than any database's own proprietary format
Parquet is the only known format capable of supporting nested data structures
Parquet requires no schema information at all, unlike proprietary formats
questions.explanation: The book notes proprietary formats cause "a huge performance hit... when interoperating with external tools," while "Parquet files in a data lake may be a superior option to proprietary cloud data warehouses in a polyglot tool environment."

questions.question: What core idea does Apache Arrow introduce, and what overhead does it eliminate?
options: A single binary columnar format usable both for in-memory processing and export/storage, eliminating separate serialize/deserialize steps when moving data between memory, network, and disk
Arrow is a row-based format optimized only for CSV interchange between systems
Arrow eliminates the need for any compression algorithm entirely
Arrow only works within a single programming language, with no cross-language support
questions.explanation: The book states Arrow's idea is "to rethink serialization by utilizing a binary data format that is suitable for both in-memory processing and export... This allows us to avoid the overhead of serialization and deserialization."

questions.question: What do "hybrid serialization" technologies like Apache Hudi and Iceberg add on top of plain columnar storage?
options: They combine multiple serialization techniques (e.g. row-oriented CDC capture plus columnar bulk storage) with table management features like atomic updates, time travel, and schema evolution
They replace columnar storage entirely with row-only storage
They remove the need for any compression or schema tracking whatsoever
They are simply alternate names for Parquet with no functional difference
questions.explanation: The book describes Hudi as combining "multiple serialization techniques to allow columnar database performance... while also supporting atomic, transactional updates," and Iceberg as supporting "schema evolution" and "table time travel."

questions.question: What's the difference between lossless and lossy compression, and which does data engineering analytics work typically require?
options: Lossless compression recovers an exact bit-for-bit copy on decompression; lossy compression (audio/images/video) only approximates the original — analytics work requires lossless compression for exact fidelity
Lossy compression is required for all analytics workloads, per the book
Lossless and lossy compression produce identical output, differing only in processing speed
Lossless compression is only usable for audio and video, never for structured data
questions.explanation: The book states: "Decompressing data encoded with a lossless algorithm recovers a bit-for-bit exact copy... Data engineers might deal with lossy compression... but not in serialization for analytics, where exact data fidelity is required."

questions.question: How do newer compression algorithms like Snappy, Zstandard, and LZ4 differ in priority from traditional ones like gzip and bzip2?
options: The newer generation prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over maximum compression ratio, making them popular for data lakes and columnar databases optimizing for fast query performance
The newer algorithms always achieve a strictly higher compression ratio than gzip/bzip2, with no speed trade-off
Snappy and Zstandard are lossy compression algorithms, unlike gzip
Newer algorithms can only be used with row-oriented formats like CSV
questions.explanation: The book describes this new generation as algorithms that "prioritize speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio," used to "optimize for fast query performance" in data lakes and columnar databases.

questions.question: How does the book frame the abundance of serialization formats, and what is reserialization?
options: The abundance is a significant source of pain but also a massive opportunity for performance improvements; reserialization is the conversion of data from one format to another as it moves through a pipeline
The abundance of formats has no downsides
Reserialization means keeping data in a single format forever
Reserialization is a storage-only concept
questions.explanation: The book describes format abundance as pain plus opportunity and defines reserialization as format conversion in pipelines.

questions.question: How must engineers handle data they are forced to accept in an "ancient, nasty form"?
options: Design processes to deserialize the format and handle exceptions, then clean up and convert the data for consistent, fast downstream processing and consumption
Reject all such data outright
Store it exactly as-is forever
Ignore exceptions during processing
questions.explanation: The book recommends deserialization with exception handling and cleaning/conversion for downstream use.

questions.question: How does the book describe CSV as a serialization format?
options: The term CSV is essentially a catchall for delimited text with flexibility in escaping, quote characters, and delimiter conventions; engineers are often required to use it to exchange data with systems outside their control, and it's common for archival
CSV has a single strict standard definition
CSV cannot be used for archival
CSV is only used for data already inside a warehouse
questions.explanation: The book describes CSV's flexibility and its forced use for external exchange and archival.

questions.question: What should you include if you use CSV for archival, and why?
options: A complete technical description of the serialization configuration for your files so that future consumers can ingest the data
A password to protect the files
Nothing — CSV is self-describing
Only the file creation date
questions.explanation: The book says archival CSV should include a complete technical description of the serialization configuration.

questions.question: What does the book say about XML as a serialization format?
options: XML was popular when HTML and the internet were new but is now viewed as legacy; it is generally slow to serialize and deserialize for data engineering, and engineers are often forced to interact with it via legacy systems — JSON has largely replaced it for plain-text object serialization
XML is the modern standard for object serialization
XML is always faster than JSON
XML is never used with legacy systems
questions.explanation: The book describes XML as legacy, slow, and largely replaced by JSON.

questions.question: How does the book describe JSON's popularity and database support?
options: JSON has emerged as the new standard for data exchange over APIs and become an extremely popular storage format; its popularity grew with MongoDB and document stores, and databases such as Snowflake, BigQuery, and SQL Server offer extensive native support
JSON is only used for APIs and never storage
JSON is not supported by cloud databases
JSON popularity is declining
questions.explanation: The book describes JSON's API/storage popularity and native database support.

questions.question: What is JSON Lines (JSONL), and when is it especially useful?
options: JSONL stores a sequence of JSON objects delimited by line breaks, and is extremely useful for storing data right after it is ingested from APIs or applications — though many columnar formats offer significantly better performance, so consider moving for intermediate pipeline stages and serving
JSONL stores a single huge JSON document
JSONL is the fastest format for serving
JSONL cannot be used for bulk semistructured data
questions.explanation: The book describes JSONL's line-delimited objects and its post-ingestion usefulness with a performance caveat.

questions.question: What is Avro, and where is it popular?
options: Avro is a row-oriented data format designed for RPCs and data serialization, encoding data into a binary format with schema metadata specified in JSON; it is popular in the Hadoop ecosystem and supported by various cloud data tools
Avro is a columnar format for analytics
Avro stores schema in XML only
Avro is exclusive to Snowflake
questions.explanation: The book describes Avro as a binary, JSON-schema row-oriented format popular in Hadoop.

questions.question: What is one obvious advantage of columnar storage that the book highlights?
options: It allows reading data from only a subset of fields rather than full rows at once — a common scenario in analytics that can dramatically reduce the amount of data scanned to execute a query
It always reads every field in every row
It requires full-row reads for all queries
It makes analytics queries scan more data
questions.explanation: The book highlights columnar storage's subset-field reads reducing scanned data.

questions.question: What compression technique does the book describe for columns with large numbers of repeated values?
options: Looking for repeated values and tokenizing them — a simple but highly efficient compression method
Encrypting each value separately
Storing every value in full with no encoding
Deleting duplicate rows permanently
questions.explanation: The book describes tokenizing repeated values as an efficient column compression technique.

questions.question: How does the book illustrate high redundancy even in columns without many exact repeated values?
options: Customer support messages organized into a single column likely show the same themes and verbiage again and again, allowing compression algorithms to realize a high ratio
Support messages never share themes
Redundancy only occurs with exact duplicates
Compression cannot exploit thematic similarity
questions.explanation: The book uses the customer-support-messages example to show high redundancy in columns.

questions.question: How do columnar databases avoid rewriting full columns on each update, and what remains true about single-row updates?
options: Columns are broken into many files, typically using partitioning and clustering strategies that organize data by query and update patterns — even so, the overhead for updating a single row is horrendous, making columnar databases a terrible fit for transactional workloads
Full columns are always rewritten on every update
Single-row updates are cheap in columnar databases
Columnar databases are ideal for transactional workloads
questions.explanation: The book describes partitioning/clustering to avoid full-column rewrites while still calling single-row updates horrendous.

questions.question: What problems does the book say Parquet solves, and what compression is especially popular with it?
options: Parquet builds in schema information, natively supports nested data unlike CSV, and is portable; speed-optimized compression algorithms such as Snappy are especially popular with it
Parquet cannot store schema information
Parquet does not support nested data
Parquet requires proprietary tools to read
questions.explanation: The book describes Parquet's schema/nesting support, portability, and Snappy's popularity.

questions.question: How does the book compare ORC to Parquet, and what limitation do cloud tools have with ORC?
options: ORC is a columnar format similar to Parquet, was very popular for Apache Hive, and is seen much less now with somewhat less support — for example, Snowflake and BigQuery can read ORC files but neither can export to ORC, while they support Parquet import and export
ORC is a row-based format
ORC has better cloud support than Parquet
BigQuery and Snowflake can export to ORC
questions.explanation: The book contrasts ORC's declining usage and the import-only limitation in cloud tools.

questions.question: How does Apache Arrow handle nested data using shredding?
options: Shredding maps each location in the schema of JSON documents into a separate column
Shredding deletes nested structures
Shredding converts all data to row format
Shredding is exclusive to CSV processing
questions.explanation: The book describes shredding as mapping each JSON schema location into a separate column.

questions.question: What in-memory advantage does Arrow's format enable for querying?
options: A data file can be stored on disk, swapped directly into program address space using virtual memory, and queried without deserialization overhead — chunks can be swapped in and out while scanning to avoid running out of memory for large datasets
Files must always be fully deserialized before querying
Virtual memory cannot be used for data files
Chunk swapping always causes out-of-memory errors
questions.explanation: The book describes Arrow's memory-mapped querying without deserialization.

questions.question: How does the Arrow project address the fact that different languages serialize data differently?
options: It provides software libraries for a variety of languages (C, Go, Java, JavaScript, MATLAB, Python, R, and Rust) that interoperate with Arrow data in memory, sometimes using interfaces to low-level code in another language, allowing cross-language interop without serialization overhead
Arrow only supports one programming language
Arrow requires serialization between all languages
Arrow cannot be used with Python
questions.explanation: The book describes Arrow's multi-language libraries enabling overhead-free interop.

questions.question: What uptake does the book note for Arrow, and what product is built around it?
options: Arrow is seeing rapid uptake with frameworks like Apache Spark, and has spanned a new data warehouse product — Dremio, a query engine and warehouse built around Arrow serialization
Arrow has no framework uptake
Dremio is built around CSV
Arrow is not used in any warehouse
questions.explanation: The book notes Spark uptake and the Arrow-based Dremio warehouse.

questions.question: What is Hudi, and how does it combine serialization techniques for a typical CDC use case?
options: Hudi (Hadoop Update Delete Incremental) combines multiple serialization techniques so a CDC stream is captured into a row-oriented format while the bulk of the table is retained in a columnar format, with a periodic repacking process combining files into updated columnar files for query efficiency
Hudi only stores row-oriented data
Hudi never repacks files
Hudi cannot be updated from CDC streams
questions.explanation: The book describes Hudi's row-oriented CDC capture plus columnar bulk storage and repacking.

questions.question: What does the book say about database storage engines?
options: All databases have an underlying storage engine; many don't expose it as a separate abstraction (e.g. BigQuery, Snowflake), some support pluggable engines (MySQL), and others offer major configuration options like columnar versus row-based storage; the storage engine is typically a separate layer from the query engine managing serialization, physical arrangement, and indexes
Databases do not have storage engines
Storage engines are always exposed to users
Storage engines never manage serialization
questions.explanation: The book describes storage engines' hidden/pluggable/configurable nature and their responsibilities.

questions.question: What storage engine innovations does the book highlight from the 2000s and 2010s?
options: Modern storage engines are better optimized for SSD performance, offer improved support for modern types and structures like variable-length strings, arrays, and nested data, and have shifted toward columnar storage for analytics — with SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL offering robust columnar support
Storage engines are still optimized for spinning disks
Columnar support is exclusive to cloud warehouses
Modern types are unsupported by storage engines
questions.explanation: The book describes SSD optimization, modern-type support, and columnar shifts in storage engines.
